sentenceText: Their first experiment showed that the more bystanders there were, the more an individual’s sense of responsibility diffused—85% of participants helped in a one-on-one situation, while only 31% did so in a group of six.
They pointed out that the bystander effect mainly springs from people’s failure to interpret a situation as an emergency due to others’ inaction.

Recent research has cast doubt on the universality of Darley and Latané’s classic bystander effect theory.

Their findings showed that bystanders intervened in 91% of cases, and in direct contradiction to the original theory, the presence of more bystanders actually increased the likelihood of intervention, with multiple people often stepping in together.
The consistent types of intervention across different cities suggest we are born with the wish to help others, driven by social conventions and a desire to understand, protect, and assist others.

What I heard was slow, forceful footsteps mixed with crying, as if someone were pacing with the weight of the world on their shoulders.
I posted in the building’s group chat, “Can the 3C neighbor keep it down after 10?” Almost immediately, Lena, a cashier at a local market, replied, “Same here.
A few others responded, but 3C never did.
“That’s it,” I thought aloud, pulling on my slippers.
